You may NOT read Python source. TOOLING (already built, use it): node /workspace/tools/probe.mjs -e 'line1\nline2' -> converts ONE snippet (backslash escapes \n \t interpreted), prints INPUT_JSON / OUTPUT_JSON / OUTPUT_RAW node /workspace/tools/probe.mjs --file snips.json -> BATCH: file holds a JSON array of strings; prints JSON [{input, output}]. STRONGLY PREFER THIS - one process per snippet is slow (~1s each), so batch 30-60 snippets per call. node /workspace/tools/probe.mjs --full a b c d e -> the whole 5-arg program output Write your batch files under /workspace/probes/-N.json (mkdir -p first). Build them with a heredoc or with node -e writing JSON, so newlines/quotes survive exactly. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT ON THE VALUES YOU PROBE: the executable uses argparse, so a snippet that starts with '-' and contains NO space (e.g. '---', '-x') is rejected as an unknown option. Work around it by putting a leading newline (e.g. '\n---') or a space, and note the workaround in your report - do not report it as a markdown behavior. YOUR JOB: produce an implementation-grade specification of your assigned area, precise enough that another engineer can reimplement it in JavaScript WITHOUT any regular expressions (manual character scanning only) and match Python-Markdown byte for byte. That means: - State the ALGORITHM (scan order, what terminates a construct, precedence vs other constructs), not just examples. - Give exact output strings including newline placement (the serializer inserts newlines in specific places). - Probe the boundaries: 0/1/2/3/4+ spaces of indentation, tabs, blank lines, EOF without trailing newline, empty content, unicode (CJK) content, interaction with adjacent constructs, malformed input. - Every rule you state MUST be backed by at least one probe you actually ran. Never guess. If you are unsure, probe. - Report verbatim JSON input/output pairs for the decisive cases (use the OUTPUT_JSON form so whitespace is visible). Budget: run at least 150 distinct probe snippets. Be exhaustive; token cost is not a concern. AREA: inline code spans (backticks) - HIGH PRIORITY, the sample tests depend on it. Let B mean a single backtick character. Cover: single B pairs; double/triple/quadruple B fences (n opening backticks close with exactly n, not fewer/more); content spanning multiple newlines inside a paragraph (a triple-backtick "fence" is parsed as an inline code span, since fenced_code is an extension and is NOT enabled!); whether leading/trailing spaces inside the span are stripped; an empty span (two adjacent backticks); the case B B space B space B B (double-fence containing a lone backtick); a lone unmatched backtick; an escaped backtick (backslash then backtick); HTML escaping inside a span (&, <, >, double quote, single quote); named/numeric entities inside a span; a backtick run at the very start of a paragraph; TWO fence-like blocks in the same paragraph separated by other text - reproduce and explain the strange nested 'bash' output shown in the task description's Test Case 3; what happens across a blank line (spans cannot cross block boundaries); a ```lang / code / ``` block as its OWN paragraph vs joined with other lines into one paragraph. input.algorithm:
## 0. Where code spans live in the pipeline Code spans are an INLINE pattern. They are resolved per-block, after block parsing, and they are the FIRST inline pattern applied (Python-Markdown registers `backtick` at priority 190, above `escape` 180, `reference` 170, `link` 160, `image_link` 150, `autolink`/`html` ~90/120, `em_strong` ~60, `linebreak` 7). Python-Markdown applies inline patterns ONE PATTERN AT A TIME over the WHOLE block text: pattern P is applied repeatedly (left-to-right, restarting after the text it just replaced) until it no longer matches anywhere, and only THEN pattern P+1 runs. Consequence: EVERY code span in a block is found before any link, emphasis, escape, autolink or raw-HTML inline is even looked at. Each match is replaced in the text by an opaque placeholder (`\x02klzzwxh:N\x03`, contains no backtick and no backslash) and the produced node is stashed; the stashed `` text is an `AtomicString`, so no later inline pattern ever re-enters it. ### Preprocessing that happens BEFORE the code-span scanner sees anything (all of it affects code spans) Given the raw document `text`: 1. Delete every U+0002 (STX) and U+0003 (ETX) character. 2. `\r\n` -> `\n`, then lone `\r` -> `\n`. 3. Append `"\n\n"`. 4. Expand tabs with tab-size 4: walk the string keeping a column counter that RESETS to 0 on `\n`; a `\t` is replaced by `(4 - column % 4)` spaces. (`\v`, `\f`, U+0085, U+2028 do NOT reset the column.) 5. Blank out space-only lines: any maximal run of ASCII spaces (U+0020 only) that is immediately preceded by `\n` and immediately followed by `\n` is deleted. NOTE: a run at offset 0 of the document is NOT preceded by `\n`, so it is not deleted. Only ASCII space counts — a line consisting of one U+00A0 or U+3000 is NOT blanked. 6. Raw HTML block extraction: block-level HTML found at the beginning of a line (indent < 4) is removed from the line stream and replaced by its own stand-alone placeholder block. This SPLITS the surrounding paragraph and therefore can destroy a would-be code span (see rules). 7. Blocks are split on blank lines. A paragraph block's inline source is `block.lstrip()` — LEFT strip only, using Python's full-Unicode whitespace set. Trailing whitespace of a block is PRESERVED. Interior line indentation is PRESERVED. ## 1. The code-span scanner (exact, regex-free) The reference implementation is the Python regex, compiled with `re.DOTALL`: (?:(? node with text = codeEscape(pyStrip(content)) i = e + n; lit = i; prevIsBackslash = false matched = true; break if matched: break if matched: continue # no n worked -> this backtick is literal; advance ONE char. i += 1; prevIsBackslash = false # (prev char is now a backtick, not '\') continue # ---------- ordinary character ---------- prevIsBackslash = (ch == '\\') i += 1 emit literal data[lit .. len(data)) return out ``` Notes that make the loop exactly equal to the regex: * Branch A simplification: because every character in `data[i..j)` is a backslash, the greedy `(?:\\{2})+` can only satisfy the `(?=`+)` lookahead when it consumes the ENTIRE run, i.e. when the run length is even and the next char is a backtick. Odd runs never match Branch A. * Branch A consumes only the backslashes; the lookahead consumes nothing, so scanning resumes AT the backtick. * Branch A's payload: `group(1).replace('\\\\', ESCAPED_BSLASH)` — each PAIR of backslashes becomes ONE literal backslash in the output (4 backslashes -> 2, 6 -> 3, 10 -> 5). * The `for n = R down to 1` / `for e ascending` nesting is the regex backtracking order and IS observable (see gotchas): a longer opening run always wins over a shorter one at the same start index, even if the shorter one would also match. * Content is `.+?` so it must be at least ONE character; a closing run therefore can never be adjacent to the opening run. `.` matches `\n` (DOTALL), so content freely spans lines *within the block*. * Because of `(?` (the XHTML serializer only self-closes tags in the HTML_EMPTY set; `code` is not in it). ## 3. codeEscape(text) Exactly three replacements, in this order: 1. `&` -> `&` 2. `<` -> `<` 3. `>` -> `>` Nothing else is escaped: `"`, `'`, `\`, `*`, `_`, `[`, `]`, `|`, `$`, `#`, `~`, backtick, CJK, emoji all pass through verbatim. Named/numeric entities are NOT decoded and NOT preserved — the `&` of `&` / `A` / ` ` is escaped, giving `&`, `A`, ` `. The XHTML serializer later runs `_escape_cdata`, which escapes `&` only when it does NOT begin an entity (`&name;`, `&#NNN;`, `&#xHH;`, case-insensitive) and escapes `<`/`>`. Since codeEscape already produced `&`/`<`/`>`, that second pass is a no-op — the net observable escaping is exactly the three replacements above. An implementer should simply apply the three replacements and emit the result raw. ## 4. Emission / newline placement `` is inline: the serializer and the `prettify` treeprocessor insert NO newlines around, inside, or after it. The span renders as the literal 6+N+7 byte sequence `` + escaped-content + `` inline in the parent's text. Newlines that were inside the content survive verbatim (`a\nb`). Container newlines are entirely a property of the containing block (`

...

`, `

...

`, `
  • ...
    • ` etc.). ## 5. Interaction summary (precedence) * Backtick beats backslash-escape: `` `a\`b` `` -> `a\b` + a stray backtick. * Backtick beats link/image/emphasis/autolink/raw-inline-HTML: a span may straddle `](`, `*`, `<...>`. * Backtick loses to everything done BEFORE inline processing: blank lines, ATX/setext headings, `---`/`===`, `>` blockquote prefixes, 4-space indented code blocks, and raw-HTML-block extraction all cut the text into blocks first, and a span cannot cross a block boundary. * Backtick does NOT lose to a `-` list marker on a continuation line (a list cannot interrupt a paragraph in core Python-Markdown), so `` `a\n- b\nc` `` stays one span. * `` ` `` at start of a paragraph is not special in any way; the paragraph's leading whitespace was already lstripped.

The opening backtick run BACKTRACKS. Almost every hand-written scanner takes the maximal run as fixed and gives up when no equal-length closing run exists. Python-Markdown instead retries with n-1, n-2, ... 1. "````a``" -> ``a, "```a``" -> `a, "`` a ` b" -> ` a b.

Greedy-opening beats lazy-content: at the same start index, n=2 is tried before n=1, so "``a`b``" gives a`b, NOT a followed by literal 'b``'. Get the loop nesting backwards and you produce different, plausible-looking output.

Content must be at least ONE character, so "``" is never an empty span and "````" never matches. But content that is only whitespace IS legal and strips to "", giving the literal string . Two different notions of "empty".

Content can never END with a backtick (negative lookbehind on the closing run), and a closing run can never be FOLLOWED by a backtick (negative lookahead). These two lookarounds, not "exactly n backticks", are what kill most malformed inputs: "`a``" and "``a```" both produce no span at all.

The strip is Python str.strip(), not a trim of one space. It removes ALL leading/trailing Unicode whitespace including newlines, U+000B, U+000C, U+001C-U+001F, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000-U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000. It does NOT remove U+200B, U+FEFF, U+00AD, U+180E, U+2060. CommonMark's rule (strip exactly one space from each side only if both sides have one and content isn't all spaces) is completely different and will mismatch on "`  code  `", "` a`" and "`a `".

Tabs are expanded to 4-column tab stops over the ENTIRE source before parsing, and the column count includes the backtick characters themselves. "`a\tb`" -> a b (2 spaces), "`abc\td`" -> abc d (4 spaces). The counter resets only on \n, not on \v/\f.

A line consisting solely of ASCII spaces is turned into a truly blank line, so it terminates the paragraph and kills a multi-line span. A line of NBSP or U+3000 does not. A line of tabs does (they become spaces first).

Escaping inside a span is only & < >, applied with & FIRST. Quotes are untouched. Entities are NOT recognised: `&` becomes &amp;. Do NOT run a generic HTML escaper that also handles " and ', and do NOT try to preserve existing entities.

The two-space line-break rule does not apply inside a span (backtick priority 190 vs linebreak priority 7), so "`a \nb`" keeps the two spaces and the newline verbatim, with no

Backslash escapes lose to backticks. "`a\\`b`" produces a\ followed by literal 'b`' — the span happily eats the backslash and closes on the "escaped" backtick. Only a backslash immediately BEFORE the opening run blocks the span.

There is a whole second alternative in the pattern for runs of backslashes: an EVEN-length backslash run immediately followed by a backtick is consumed separately, collapsing each pair to one literal backslash and clearing the way for the span ("\\\\`x`" -> \x). An ODD-length run does not take that path at all ("\\\\\\`x`" -> \`x`). Off-by-one here changes both the backslash count and whether a span forms.

Leftmost-match, not best-match. In "`x`` y `` z" the scanner tries index 0 (n=1) first, exhausts every closing candidate, fails, and only then matches at index 2 — leaving the literal '`x' at the front of the output. Adding a single backtick later in the same line ("`x`` y `` z ` w") flips the whole parse to x`` y `` z.

Block structure wins over spans. Blank lines, setext underlines (--- / ===), ATX headings, 4-space indented lines and any line-initial block-level raw HTML all cut the text before the span scanner runs.
